Selecting negatives by current model score without logQ correction changes sampled-candidate cross entropy into a sampler-dependent ranking surrogate; it generally does not estimate full-catalog softmax faithfully. Frequently selected items receive more negative pressure, altering the tradeoff between popular and rare items ([Rawat et al., 2021](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v139/rawat21a.html)). Hard-negative sampling can nevertheless improve top-K ranking: a theoretical connection to partial AUC exists for BPR, although that result does not directly establish equivalence for candidate cross entropy ([Shi et al., 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.03472)). LogQ correction must reflect the actual sampling mechanism; finite-sample bias can remain, and an always-included positive requires different treatment from sampled negatives ([Khrylchenko et al., 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09331)).

Direct algebraic consequence of retaining duplicates: if negative item j occurs m times, its denominator contribution is m·exp(s_j), equivalent to one entry with logit s_j+log(m). Duplicates therefore impose multiplicity weighting and reduce unique candidate coverage; their total gradient contribution increases, though normalization prevents a simple m-fold gradient increase. Repeated draws are legitimate under a with-replacement importance estimator, but uncorrected duplicates emphasize the sampler’s preferences. Deduplication changes sampling probabilities and requires corresponding correction when approximating full softmax. Separately, high-scoring unobserved items may be genuine future positives; repeatedly penalizing them amplifies false-negative harm ([Chen et al., 2022](https://doi.org/10.1145/3522672)). For this benchmark, duplicate-heavy training also differs from evaluation against 99 unique negatives; any benefit should be established using the fixed validation protocol.
